What the Fourier Transform Tells Us (and What It Doesn’t)

We are halfway through the semester! Next week, we are going to transition to linear algebra—finally, something a little different from calculus. No more derivatives or integrals for a bit. But before we leave our current topic behind, let’s summarize what we actually gain by taking a Fourier transform of a complicated time-domain waveform.

When we feed a time-domain signal x(t) into a Fourier transform, we get a frequency-domain spectrum X(f). There are three main pieces of information we can extract from this:

  1. Frequencies (Harmonics): We find out exactly what resonant frequencies are present in the signal.

  2. Amplitude: We don’t just know if a frequency is there; we know how big each frequency component is relative to the others.

  3. Damping (or Decay): Remember the borderline inappropriate joke I told you? If you have a purely undamped sine wave, its Fourier transform is one infinitely sharp peak—like a middle finger sticking straight up. But in the real world, signals decay. This damping causes that sharp peak to smear out and become broader. By looking at the width of the peak, we can quantify the damping of the physical system.

What do we lose? Phase shift. The magnitude of the Fourier transform tells us nothing about how the wave is shifted in time. We lose the relative phase information of the original waveform.

Free Induction Decay (FID) in NMR

Let’s bring this concept back to Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR). In modern NMR, we don’t just continuously blast the sample with an AC magnetic field (like they did back in the 1960s). Instead, we hit the sample with a short pulse of magnetic field to excite the nuclear spins, and then we just listen. We let the signal ring.

As the nuclear spins precess, their changing magnetic field induces a time-varying voltage in our pickup coils. It is exactly the same principle as the pickups on an electric guitar! Because we just hit the system once and let it decay freely without further interference, this recorded signal is called a Free Induction Decay (FID).

Eventually, this signal dies out. And because the time-domain signal decays, its Fourier transform will not be an infinitely sharp line. It will have some width to it. The physical mechanisms causing this decay dictate the shape and width of the peaks in our NMR spectrum.

Decay Mechanisms: Damping vs. Dephasing

Why does the NMR signal decay? You might immediately think of damping, like friction. If you have a precessing top, friction eventually causes it to fall down. Nuclear spins can experience a similar type of damping, but it’s sort of the opposite: as they precess, they eventually get “sucked in” toward the direction of the main external magnetic field (B_0), standing more upright until they stop precessing in the transverse plane. This process is called damping (or spin-lattice relaxation), and it happens over a timescale we call T_1.

But there is another, often much faster, way the signal can decay. It’s not that the spins stop precessing—they keep going! But remember, our pickup coils are measuring the collective signal of an enormous ensemble of spins. If each spin experiences a slightly different local magnetic field, they will precess at slightly different frequencies. Over time, they drift out of sync with each other. They lose their lockstep. This process is called dephasing (or spin-spin relaxation), and it happens over a timescale we call T_2.

Because dephasing (T_2) usually happens faster than damping (T_1), it is typically the dominant process that smears out our signal and broadens our NMR peaks.

If we somehow found a magical system where T_1 was one millisecond and T_2 was ten seconds, which mechanism would dictate the width of our NMR peak?

In that unusual case, damping (T_1) would dominate the peak broadening. The rule is that whichever decay process happens faster is the one that primarily smears out the signal. Since T_1 is much shorter here, the spins would stand upright long before they had a chance to drift out of sync!

The Molecular Environment: Free vs. Bound

To really understand dephasing, let’s look at a practical example. Suppose we have the exact same molecule in two different environments: freely tumbling in a liquid, versus anchored to a large gold nanoparticle.

Which one gives a sharper NMR peak? Counterintuitively, it is the freely tumbling molecules!

Why does the chaotic liquid environment produce a sharper peak? It comes down to timescales. In a liquid, small molecules tumble incredibly fast—on the order of picoseconds. As they tumble, the local magnetic field felt by any given hydrogen nucleus fluctuates wildly because its neighbors are constantly moving around. Naively, you would think this chaos would cause massive dephasing.

But the fluctuations are so fast compared to the timescale of our NMR measurement (which is in milliseconds) that they average out to zero! The spins do not have time to accumulate any meaningful phase difference before the local field flips again. They stay in step. This phenomenon is called motional narrowing.

Now, what happens when we attach that same molecule to a nanoparticle? The nanoparticle is huge, so it tumbles much, much more slowly. The local magnetic field fluctuations no longer average out. Each nuclear spin is stuck feeling a slightly different local field for a long enough time that their precession frequencies fan apart. They dephase. The collective signal decays faster (resulting in a shorter T_2), and the resulting frequency peak is broad and smeared out.

This is an incredibly useful diagnostic tool in nanoscience. If you want to know whether your molecules successfully attached to your nanoparticles, you just run an NMR scan. If you see sharp peaks, they are still floating freely. If the peaks broaden out, congratulations—you have successfully functionalized your nanoparticles!

Imagine you run an NMR scan on a batch of nanoparticles, but the resulting spectrum shows very sharp, narrow peaks. What does this tell you about your sample?

Sharp peaks indicate that the molecules are tumbling very rapidly, meaning they are likely just floating freely in the liquid. This tells you that your attempt to attach them to the heavy, slow-tumbling nanoparticles probably failed. You will need to head back to the fume hood and try your functionalization reaction again!

Quantifying Linewidth and the Lorentzian Fit

We keep talking about peaks being “sharp” or “broad”. Let’s put some rigorous math to this. The width of our spectral peak is called the linewidth.

When a signal decays exponentially in the time domain—like our FID with time constant T_2—its Fourier transform takes on a very specific mathematical shape called a Lorentzian function. We can write the Lorentzian profile L(f) as:

\begin{equation} \tag{1} L(f) = \frac{A}{\pi} \frac{\gamma}{(f - f_0)^2 + \gamma^2} \end{equation}

Here, A is a scaling factor for the overall area of the peak, f_0 is the center resonant frequency, and \gamma is a parameter known as the Half-Width at Half-Maximum (HWHM). The HWHM is exactly what it sounds like: if you find the maximum height of the peak and go halfway down to the baseline, \gamma is the width from the center frequency out to that edge.

In spectroscopy, we often talk about the Full-Width at Half-Maximum (FWHM), denoted as \Delta \nu. Because the Lorentzian function is symmetric, the FWHM is simply twice the HWHM:

\begin{equation} \tag{2} \Delta \nu = 2\gamma \end{equation}

How does this tie back to our physical system? The faster the spins dephase, the faster the signal decays, and the broader the resulting peak. The exact mathematical relationship between the FWHM linewidth and the dephasing time T_2 is given by:

\begin{equation} \tag{3} \Delta \nu = \frac{1}{\pi T_2} \end{equation}

By combining Equation 2 and Equation 3, we can see that the HWHM \gamma is directly related to the dephasing time by \gamma = 1/(2\pi T_2). So, if you measure the linewidth from your NMR spectrum, you can immediately calculate how fast your spins are losing synchrony! A short T_2 means a broad line, and a long T_2 means a sharp line.

You measure an NMR spectrum and find that a specific peak has a Full-Width at Half-Maximum (FWHM) of 10 Hz. Roughly how long is the dephasing time T_2 for these spins?

We can rearrange our linewidth equation to solve for the dephasing time as T_2 = 1 / (\pi \Delta \nu). Plugging in a linewidth of 10 Hz, we get T_2 = 1 / (10\pi), which is approximately 0.032 seconds, or 32 milliseconds. This gives us a direct, quantitative measure of how fast the spins are losing their phase coherence!
